PROJECT DELIVERY & BUSINESS OPERATIONS

Real Results From My Work

1. Legal Technology Spend Consolidation | K2 Services

Project Manager K2

PROBLEM
Practice groups had independently purchased 27 legal technology subscriptions. Most auto-renewed, usage wasn't centrally tracked, and several tools overlapped.
ACTION
Inventoried all 27 tools with usage data, flagged 5 below 30% license use, and led practice group sessions to standardize tools by category. When Litigation raised concerns about switching mid-matter, I recommended reducing licenses from 40 to 10 instead and introduced a 120-day pre-renewal review.
RESULT
Retired 4 redundant tools and right-sized 3 others, cutting annual spend by $146K (11%).
LESSON
Standardization creates resistance when it ignores how teams actually work. A targeted exception preserved stakeholder trust while capturing most of the available savings.

2. AI Student Services Assistant | Central Michigan University

Assistant Project Manager · Central Michigan University

PROBLEM
Each August, approximately 11,000 calls hit three student service offices in four weeks, and 38% of callers abandoned the queue before reaching anyone.
ACTION
Owned the launch plan and content audit for a FERPA-compliant AI assistant across three offices, flagging 140 outdated pages before launch. When the vendor reported 81% containment, I identified that it included abandoned conversations and proposed a stricter 7-day follow-up measure, which the Director of Student Systems adopted.
RESULT
46% of questions were resolved without a follow-up call within 7 days. Abandoned calls fell 38% → 14%, and average wait time dropped 22 → 9 minutes.
LESSON
A successful metric has to reflect the user experience. The vendor's metric said the launch worked; students' follow-up behavior showed whether it actually did.

3. Patient Data Conversion, Cerner-to-Epic | Robert Half

Project Coordinator · Conduent

PROBLEM
A 1.1M-record Cerner-to-Epic conversion found demographic mismatches and potential duplicates in 2.6% of records, creating patient-safety and billing risk against a fixed go-live.
ACTION
Coordinated three mock conversions across data conversion, HIM, registration, and revenue cycle, tracking findings through resolution and sign-off. When two departments disagreed about delaying go-live, I led a joint review that classified every open issue by severity and downstream impact for the steering committee.
RESULT
Mismatches fell 2.6% → 0.07%, and the conversion went live on schedule with zero critical data defects.
LESSON
Not every unresolved issue should delay delivery. The work is distinguishing tolerable risks from critical ones and giving decision-makers a clear basis for go/no-go.

HOW I WORK

My Project Delivery Framework

Cards open on hover. Tap anywhere on a card to open or keep open. Tap anywhere again to close it.

01Discover & AlignDo we understand what we're actually doing?+

Establishing context before building the planI start by understanding the project before jumping into execution. That means establishing what we’re delivering, who owns the outcome, what constraints we’re working within, who has decision-making authority, and what challenges already exist.

Key focus areas

  • Clarifying the business need, scope, deliverables, and desired outcomes
  • Identifying stakeholders, project ownership, and decision-makers
  • Establishing timelines, constraints, and success measures
  • Uncovering existing issues, risks, assumptions, and dependencies
  • Validating requirements with technical and business stakeholders

Outcome

A shared understanding of the project that allows planning to be based on validated information rather than assumptions.

02Plan & OrganizeHow are we going to deliver it?+

Turning validated requirements into a clear path to deliveryOnce the project is understood, I translate that context into an actionable plan. I establish how the work will move forward, who is responsible for what, when key milestones need to happen, and where dependencies could affect delivery.

Key focus areas

  • Building project plans, timelines, and delivery milestones
  • Defining ownership, responsibilities, and handoffs
  • Mapping dependencies and sequencing project activities
  • Planning resources, budgets, and delivery checkpoints
  • Establishing communication, reporting, and risk-management cadence

Outcome

A structured and realistic delivery plan that gives teams clear expectations, ownership, and visibility into how the project will move forward.

03Coordinate & ControlAre we staying on track?+

Maintaining visibility and momentum throughout executionOnce execution begins, I focus on keeping people, priorities, and progress aligned. I monitor the health of the project, keep stakeholders informed, follow up on commitments, and address risks or blockers before they significantly affect delivery.

Key focus areas

  • Monitoring milestones, deliverables, deadlines, and project health
  • Tracking risks, issues, dependencies, decisions, and action items
  • Coordinating technical, business, vendor, and other stakeholders
  • Managing status updates, meetings, and project documentation
  • Monitoring budget and resource activity
  • Escalating blockers and facilitating resolution when needed

Outcome

A well-coordinated project where stakeholders have visibility, responsibilities remain clear, and emerging issues are addressed before they derail delivery.

04Launch, Transition & ImproveIs it ready to operate successfully?+

Turning successful delivery into sustainable operationsAs the project approaches completion, I focus on making sure the solution is actually ready to launch, transition, and operate successfully. That includes validating readiness, resolving outstanding issues, coordinating handoffs, and capturing what can be improved going forward.

Key focus areas

  • Coordinating implementation and launch-readiness activities
  • Supporting testing, validation, and user acceptance
  • Tracking and resolving outstanding launch issues
  • Preparing operational handoffs and supporting documentation
  • Monitoring post-launch needs and follow-up activities
  • Capturing lessons learned and process-improvement opportunities

Outcome

A controlled transition from project delivery into day-to-day operations, with the documentation, ownership, and follow-through needed to support long-term success.

PROJECT SIMULATIONS

Case Studies

Three project scenarios showing how I plan, coordinate, and make delivery decisions. Outcomes below are targets.

TECHNOLOGY · SaaS · SECURITY COMPLIANCE

SOC 2 Type II Readiness for Enterprise Sales

Timeline9 months
Budget$185,000
TeamSolo PM + 7 control owners

The challenge

Lumenly, a 120-person HR software company, was losing enterprise deals because buyers required a SOC 2 Type II report, with $2.3M in sales pipeline waiting on completion. Readiness required implementing and operating 64 controls across five departments before entering the audit observation period.

My role & approach

Led the program from kickoff through audit readiness as the sole PM. Ran the initial gap assessment, assigned owners and due dates to 23 missing controls, managed the integrated readiness plan, and coordinated weekly control-owner reviews, the compliance platform vendor, and auditor. Reported progress, risks, and decisions to the CTO and VP of Sales.

Key decision

Sales wanted the audit period to begin immediately, but quarterly access reviews and vendor risk assessments had never completed a full operating cycle. Starting early increased the risk of audit exceptions. I recommended completing one full cycle of both controls before beginning the observation period, trading six weeks of schedule for stronger audit evidence. The CTO approved the recommendation, and Sales received a firm revised report date.

Target outcomes

  • Zero significant exceptions
  • $2.3M pipeline unblocked
  • Questionnaire turnaround: 3 weeks → 3 days
  • 64/64 controls assigned and operational
Key lesson

Audit readiness is about proving controls operate consistently, not simply documenting that they exist. Protecting evidence quality justified a deliberate schedule trade-off.

NONPROFIT · COMMUNITY FINANCE · MULTI-SITE EXPANSION

Free Tax Assistance Program Expansion

Timeline14-week readiness window
Budget$210,000 grant
Team4 core members + ~65 volunteers

The challenge

Bridgewater Community Action operated free IRS VITA tax preparation across six sites. A new grant funded expansion to 14 sites in a single filing season, requiring each location to secure a host, certified volunteers, quality reviewers, equipment, and appointment capacity before opening. The expansion also needed to reach more households eligible for the Earned Income Tax Credit.

My role & approach

Owned the expansion plan, budget, site-readiness tracking, volunteer certification coordination, and weekly reporting to the Executive Director and grant officer. Established a nine-criterion readiness gate and sequenced the 14 locations into three launch groups, allowing each site to open only after meeting its readiness requirements.

Key decision

Initial locations were influenced by existing board relationships. I compared the proposed sites against EITC-eligible household concentrations and transit access and found that three proposed locations served lower-need areas while two high-need neighborhoods lacked coverage. I recommended replacing three proposed sites with locations better aligned to community need and accessibility. The board approved the revised footprint.

Target outcomes

  • 14 sites ready for filing season
  • 4,200 returns vs. 2,300 baseline
  • $5.1M in refunds and credits returned
  • 95%+ return accuracy
Key lesson

Site selection should optimize access to the intended population, not organizational convenience. Defining objective selection criteria made a politically sensitive decision defensible.

FINANCE · CAPITAL MARKETS · REGULATORY CHANGE

Trade Settlement Transition to T+1

Timeline6 months
Budget$340,000
TeamSolo PM + 4 functional leads

The challenge

Halvorsen Securities had to transition from T+2 to T+1 settlement by a fixed industry deadline. Allocations, confirmations, and affirmations now needed to occur on trade date, increasing the operational risk of late affirmations and failed trades. Only 61% of trades were being affirmed the same day at baseline.

My role & approach

Owned the transition plan, RAID log, testing schedule, and executive readiness reporting to the COO. Mapped the trade lifecycle by hour, established daily same-day affirmation reporting by client, coordinated dependencies across four functional leads and three custodian banks, and managed four testing cycles before cutover.

Key decision

Technology proposed purchasing a new matching platform to improve affirmation speed. Before committing the spend, I used the daily affirmation analysis to isolate the source of delays. Five clients accounted for 72% of late affirmations, primarily because allocations arrived after 6 p.m. I recommended earlier allocation cutoffs and targeted operations outreach before pursuing a technology replacement. The COO approved the recommendation and deferred the platform decision.

Target outcomes

  • Same-day affirmation: 61% → 93%
  • Fail rate <1% in month one
  • Zero regulatory findings
  • ~$400K platform investment avoided
Key lesson

Diagnose the constraint before investing in the solution. Process-level data can distinguish a technology problem from an upstream workflow problem and prevent unnecessary spend.
